Lessons.Title: The Commutative Property
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: explain and use the commutative property of multiplication by reading and writing two full equations for an array, including its group orientations. This first-party lesson is source-aligned to the IM K–5 2021 first edition U01 L20; original publisher images are not copied.

Number Talk, Subtraction (10 minutes): solve 70−10=60, 68−10=58, 70−12=58 and 68−12=56. Think mentally using tens/ones place value and explain a strategy; students are developing fluency and reasoning, and the teacher reviews methods, not only correct numbers.

Activity 1, Learn More About Multiplication (20 minutes): original Image A illustrates two groups of five and Image B five groups of two. Both contain ten dots, but the group relationships differ. Students first notice and wonder, compose a situation for each image, compare the situation meanings and then write BOTH complete equations 2×5=10 and 5×2=10. They explain what each factor and the product mean, with MLR8 discussion and attention to visual grouping. A pair of numeric products alone is not evidence that the student interpreted the original images.

Activity 2, Revisit Arrays (15 minutes): look at the original array of three groups of six (18), write both 3×6=18 and 6×3=18, and explain two ways of grouping the same array. Use source MLR1 Stronger and Clearer Each Time to exchange explanations with multiple partners and revise the text. Machine grading requires two complete true equations with correctly swapped factors; the source drawing and explanation remain teacher-judged.

Lesson synthesis (10 minutes): compare a 3-by-4 array as 3×4=12 and 4×3=12, then explain why 3×4=4×3. Name this the commutative property: changing the factor order does not change the product. The source section summary further contrasts drawings, arrays, multiplication expressions and complete multiplication equations (e.g., 3×5 versus 3×5=15).

Cool-down (5 minutes): original publisher Multiplication Reflection prompt is gated for educators. Edulytics's separate first-party task uses 4×6=24 and 6×4=24 to assess the complete-pair skill, while requiring teacher review of array drawings and explanations.

KeyConcepts.Title: Commutativity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Reversing two multiplication factors leaves the product unchanged.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For positive whole-number factors a and b, a×b=b×a.

KeyConcepts.Title: Factor roles versus total
KeyConcepts.Definition: Rows and columns may exchange group count and group size, without changing the number of objects.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Explain how factors are attached to the source image, not just the repeated product.
KeyConcepts.Example: Three groups of six and six groups of three both contain 18 objects.

KeyConcepts.Title: Full equation pair
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two complete multiplication equalities show the same product with reversed factors.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Require both equations; a single total, an expression alone, or a repeated equation does not demonstrate commutativity.

KeyConcepts.Title: Mathematical argument
KeyConcepts.Definition: An array image and conversation justify the two equal equations.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The original text must be discussed, peer-reviewed and revised in MLR1; this cannot be auto-graded.
KeyConcepts.Example: Draw a three-by-six grid and locate groups in each direction.

WorkedExamples.Title: Mental subtraction warm-up
WorkedExamples.Question: Mentally calculate 70−10, 68−10, 70−12 and 68−12.
WorkedExamples.Method: Separate tens and ones then compare related differences.

WorkedExamples.Title: Different images, same product
WorkedExamples.Question: Image A shows two groups of five; image B five groups of two. What two equations express the groups?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count the same ten dots along the two source groupings.
Steps: Image A: two equal groups of five, 2×5=10.
Image B: five equal groups of two, 5×2=10.
Compare which factor represents which type of group.
Explain to a partner why total ten is unchanged.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both original source image meanings need teacher review.

WorkedExamples.Title: Three by six revisit
WorkedExamples.Question: Write two full equations for a source array with three rows of six.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret one grouping as rows, then the other as columns.
Steps: Explain both equalities using one complete array.
Revise the explanation after MLR1 partner feedback.
WorkedExamples.Check: Digital checker assesses both equations; teacher assesses why both fit the model.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original source asks for TWO full equations with reversed factors.
This fails to display a reversal of factors.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Swap the distinct factors while retaining the product.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming the pictures have a different number of dots.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source two images both show ten dots with different orientations.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Distinguish source group structure from total.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Equating a valid equation pair with a completed oral peer critique.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Partner explanation and revision have separate source learning objectives.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher assesses MLR1 mathematical language and reflection.

SummaryPoints: Source Image A: two groups of five; Image B: five groups of two; both total 10.
Activity 1: write source array situations, compare factors and record two complete equations.
Activity 2: source 3×6=18 and 6×3=18, plus written and revised explanation using MLR1.
Synthesis uses 3×4=12, 4×3=12 and 3×4=4×3 to name the commutative property.
Section summary distinguishes drawings, arrays, multiplication expressions and equalities.
Publisher visual pixels, gated Cool-down and teacher peer-interaction evidence are separate outstanding verifications.
